A session is not finished until it is documented — and the note you write **is** the clinical record.

By the end of this lesson you can start a progress note from the right appointment, structure it clearly, keep reported information separate from what you observed, and use Splose’s AI drafting tools the safe way: as a drafting hand, never as the author of record.
steps.title: The note is the clinical record

steps.body:
Notes for a session start **from that session’s appointment** — that is what ties the note to the right client, date, service and practitioner.

In the Calendar, click the appointment, confirm those details are the ones you expect, then select **Add progress note**. Pick the appropriate progress-note template and the editor opens.

image.alt: A Splose appointment panel with client contact details hidden and the Add progress note link circled. The panel also shows the appointment time, service and note field.

steps.title: Start from the appointment

steps.body:
The note editor builds from blocks. Type **/** to open the insert menu — headings, text, bullet lists, numbered lists, and depending on configuration, tables, images and signatures.

Use headings to give the note a visible clinical structure rather than one long paragraph.

image.alt: The Splose note editor with a slash-command menu open, offering Heading 1, Heading 2, Heading 3, Text, Bullet list and Numbered list blocks.

steps.title: The editor and slash commands

steps.body:
Use the note structure Opal provides in the template — do not invent your own per note.

A classic **SOAP** structure is Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan. Opal may instead configure a practical OT structure along the lines of: presentation and reported information, intervention, observations of occupational performance, clinical interpretation, participant response, and plan.

Whichever template Opal supplies: same structure, every note — that consistency is what makes records readable across the team.
steps.title: Structure the note

steps.body:
A defensible note keeps three kinds of statement visibly distinct:

**Reported** — “Mother reported difficulty with morning routines.”
**Observed** — “OT observed the participant complete the task with verbal prompting.”
**Clinical interpretation** — “This suggests reduced task initiation.”

Never convert a collateral report into a direct observation. What a parent, teacher or support worker told you stays labelled as reported — however plausible it sounds.
steps.title: Reported. Observed. Interpreted.

steps.body:
Where Opal has AI enabled, the slash menu offers two AI options:

**Load AI block** — inserts a preconfigured prompt from the library. When Opal publishes approved prompts, this is the one you use.

**Insert AI block** — creates an empty block for a custom prompt.

Typical uses: summarising, drafting a structured section, extracting actions, or tidying rough notes. Splose can also use a session transcript as context and draft a note with **Write Progress Note**, where that capability is enabled.

image.alt: The Splose note editor slash menu showing two AI options — Load AI block, which inserts a prompt from the library, and Insert AI block, which creates an empty custom prompt — above an example AI promp

steps.title: AI blocks

steps.body:
Every AI-generated sentence is a **draft** until you have verified it. The working rule:

generate → **read all of it** → compare against the session → correct anything unsupported → add the clinical reasoning only you can supply → then finalise.

Never auto-finalise AI output. The treating practitioner remains responsible for the record — the tool never is.

Watch for the classic leap: a parent reported difficulty brushing teeth, and the draft asserts “requires moderate assistance with oral hygiene.” An assistance level belongs in the note only if it was actually established, observed or assessed.
steps.title: AI output is a draft. You are the author.

quiz.explain: Starting from the appointment ties the note to the right client, date, service and practitioner automatically — the links that make it findable and auditable later.
options: From the client’s file, whenever convenient
From that session’s appointment in the calendar
In a separate document, pasted in later
quiz.question: Where should a progress note for a specific session normally be started?

quiz.explain: You did not see it — someone told you. It stays labelled as reported, and must never drift into the note as an observation.
options: Direct observation
Clinical interpretation
Collateral / reported information
quiz.question: “Support worker reported the participant refused breakfast.” What kind of evidence is this?

quiz.explain: Load AI block loads from the library — the home of approved prompts. Insert AI block creates an empty custom block.
options: Insert AI block
Load AI block
quiz.question: Which option inserts an approved prompt from the library, rather than a custom one?

steps.title: Quick check: the two AI options

quiz.explain: The draft turned a parent’s report into an assessed assistance level — a claim nothing in the session supports. Fix the unsupported statement and keep drafting; the discipline is verification, not avoidance.
options: Keep it — it is a reasonable clinical summary
Correct it: the assistance level was never established, so it cannot stand as written
Delete the whole draft and refuse to use AI
quiz.question: Your session record says: “Parent reported difficulty brushing teeth.” The AI draft says: “Participant requires moderate assistance with oral hygiene.” What do you do?

steps.body:
Not settled yet, so not taught here: Opal’s final progress-note template, consent requirements for recording or transcribing sessions, audio retention rules, exactly which AI functions are enabled and approved, whether custom AI prompts are permitted, and note finalisation and amendment rules in Splose.

Until Opal publishes these, ask before recording any session audio and before relying on an AI feature this lesson has not covered.
steps.title: Still being finalised at Opal

steps.body:
Notes start from the appointment, follow the practice structure, keep reported and observed apart — and AI drafts only ever leave your hands after you have verified every line.

Next: connecting Splose to Teams and Outlook.
steps.title: Documentation you can stand behind

title: Notifications
description: Where alerts arrive, what each type means, and how to keep the list clean.

steps.body:
The portal keeps an eye on your day and lets you know when something needs attention: schedule clashes, expiring credentials, sync trouble, policy updates and more.

Everything arrives in one place — the notifications panel. Alerts appear inside the portal only; they are not emailed to you, so the panel is worth a glance each day. This walkthrough takes a few minutes.
steps.title: Where alerts arrive

steps.body:
The bell sits in the top bar on every page. When you have unread alerts, a red badge shows the count — it refreshes about once a minute while the portal is open.

**Click the bell** to open your notifications.
steps.title: The bell

steps.body:
Day-to-day notices arrive here: a summary of today’s appointments (on days you have any), calendar clashes, appointments missing an address, unusually long travel between visits, sessions still waiting on a case note, and reminders when a credential is close to expiry or CPD hours are behind pace.

The practice uses it too: you’ll be told when a policy in the Resource Hub changes and needs a fresh acknowledgement, and when a support ticket you reported is updated.

If there’s nothing to show, you’ll see **You’re all caught up!**
steps.title: What lands here

steps.body:
Because you help run the practice, some extra alerts come your way: clients who haven’t been seen for several weeks, client addresses the portal can’t resolve, and team members whose profiles are incomplete.

Owners also receive billing readiness notices, plus an alert whenever an automatic sync is halted as a safety precaution.
steps.title: Practice-level alerts

steps.body:
If the portal and Outlook lose touch — the regular sync has stopped moving, or a change couldn’t be written back to your Outlook calendar — a red alert appears here. Nothing is lost, but the two calendars can drift out of step until the connection is sorted, so it’s worth acting on.

Splose connection problems appear the same way, with a **Retry sync** button that re-checks the connection on the spot. Outlook alerts carry a shortcut button — **Reconnect Outlook** or **Open Integrations** — which opens Settings, where the practice owner can re-link the mailbox. That Settings page is owner-only: for everyone else, if your Outlook link has dropped, use the **Connect Outlook** banner that appears at the top of the Calendar, or ask the owner for a hand.

image.alt: A red sync alert in the notifications panel with a Reconnect Outlook button

steps.title: Sync trouble

steps.body:
Unread alerts are tinted, with a dot on the right-hand side — the bell badge counts them.

Most alerts are linked to a page: click one and it’s marked as read and the portal takes you there — a calendar clash opens the Calendar, a credential reminder opens My Profile. Many also carry a shortcut button such as **Open Profile** or **View Calendar**. Alerts without a linked page simply mark themselves read when clicked.
steps.title: Read, unread and jumping across

steps.body:
**Mark all read** clears the badge and the unread tints in one go — the alerts themselves stay in the list.

To remove an alert, use its **Dismiss** button. One thing to know: if the underlying issue is still there — say two appointments still overlap — the portal raises the alert again on a later check. Fix the issue and it stays gone. The daily schedule summary is the exception — there’s nothing to fix, so dismissing it only hides it until the panel next refreshes, and it returns on any day you have appointments.
steps.title: Keeping the list tidy

steps.body: **Click the close button** in the top corner of the panel. Clicking anywhere outside the panel, or pressing Escape, works too.
steps.title: Close the panel

steps.body:
As the practice owner you also have a Settings area with a page of notification switches.

**Click Notifications** in the settings menu to open it.
steps.title: Notification settings

steps.body:
The switches that make a visible difference today are the calendar ones: **Calendar conflict warnings** turns the red conflict badges on calendar tiles on or off, **Missing location alerts** controls the missing-address markers, and the **Dormant Cases** controls set whether dormant-case detection runs and how many quiet weeks count as dormant.

Worth knowing: these switches don’t filter the notifications panel — it always shows every alert raised for you.

If you change anything, press **Save Notification Settings** and wait for the Saved tick.
steps.title: What these switches do

steps.body:
Your own reminder preferences live behind this **Notifications** card — the same choices you made on the sign-up checklist. Toggles here save the moment you flip them.

The one to know is the **work-location reminder**: leave it on and, on Fridays, if next week’s work locations aren’t filled in, a reminder lands in your notifications panel.

An honest note: the other reminders listed on that page are recorded but not active yet, and nothing on it is emailed — alerts only ever arrive inside the portal.

image.alt: The Notifications card on the My Profile dashboard

steps.title: Your personal reminders

quiz.explain: Mark all read only clears the unread highlights — the alert stays in the list. Dismiss removes it, and because the clash is already fixed, it won’t come back.
options: Its Dismiss button
Mark all read
Closing and reopening the panel
quiz.question: You’ve fixed an overlapping appointment, but the clash alert is still sitting in the panel. What clears it out of the list?

steps.body:
You know where alerts arrive, what the main types mean, how to jump from an alert to the right page, and how to keep the list tidy with Mark all read and Dismiss.

Next, meet **Opa**, the practice’s AI sidekick — what it can and can’t do, and how to use it well.
steps.title: Alerts under control

title: Your Performance Report
description: Reading your own Splose performance report: utilisation, what the numbers do and do not mean, and why incomplete notes come first.

steps.body:
Splose can show you an honest picture of your own working week: sessions delivered, time utilised, travel, and — most importantly — any sessions still missing their notes.

By the end of this lesson you can open your own performance report, read each metric for what it actually measures, and act on the one number that is really a clinical follow-up list in disguise.
steps.title: Your numbers, read properly

steps.body:
In Splose: **Reports → Performance**.

Set the **date range** you want to look at, select **your own practitioner name**, and review the metrics for that period.
steps.title: Find your report

steps.body:
**1:1 Appointments** — one-on-one sessions marked as arrived.
**Appointments Utilisation** — the share of your available time spent in arrived appointments.
**Group attendees** — participants seen in group sessions.
**Support activities** — hours in support and non-clinical activity, depending on configuration.
**Travel** — provider travel hours.
**Total hours / Total Utilisation** — the broader picture across recognised service activity.
**Revenue** — invoiced revenue from appointments, support activities and travel.
**Cancellations** and **Incomplete notes** — the follow-up signals.
steps.title: What the metrics measure

steps.body:
Utilisation is a simple fraction of your available time.

Available time this week: **40 hours**. Time in arrived appointments: **28 hours**. Appointment utilisation: 28 ÷ 40 = **70%**.

Appointment utilisation and Total Utilisation can differ, because broader utilisation may also count other recognised service time — support activities or travel, depending on configuration.

And a caution built into the metric: utilisation measures **workload**, not clinical quality. A higher number is not a better therapist.
steps.title: The utilisation sum

steps.body:
**Incomplete notes** is not a KPI to admire — it is a list of sessions whose clinical documentation is missing.

You finished six sessions yesterday and the report shows 2 incomplete notes? That is two clinical records currently incomplete: identify which sessions they are, and complete or review the documentation promptly.
steps.title: Incomplete notes come first

quiz.explain: 28 ÷ 40 = 0.70 — seventy percent of available time in arrived appointments.
quiz.question: Available time 40 hours; arrived appointment time 28 hours. Appointment utilisation?

quiz.explain: Utilisation is an operational measure of how available time was used. Clinical quality lives in the work itself and its documentation.
options: Yes — more sessions means better care
No — utilisation measures workload, not clinical quality
quiz.question: Does high utilisation automatically mean high-quality clinical work?

steps.title: Quick check: what the number means

quiz.explain: Incomplete notes are outstanding clinical records. Find the sessions, finish the documentation — promptly, while the session is still fresh.
options: Note it and move on — it is only a statistic
Identify the sessions missing notes and complete or review the documentation promptly
Ask admin to clear the counter
quiz.question: Your report shows Incomplete notes: 2. What is the practical response?

steps.body:
Managers and owners may have access to the broader **Performance Overview**: practitioner comparisons, utilisation and revenue charts over time, and PNG / JPG / CSV export for reporting.

Use it as an operational lens across the practice. Practitioners are not expected to compare colleagues — this view is a management tool, and this step of the lesson only appears for management roles.

image.alt: The Splose Performance overview dashboard comparing utilisation and revenue over a date range, with a download menu circled offering PNG image, JPG image and CSV data export.

steps.title: Manager view: Performance Overview

quiz.explain: Your report is for your own work. Cross-practitioner comparison is a management function, used with the care any staff-level data deserves.
options: Yes — friendly competition helps
No — not unless their role and permissions specifically require it
quiz.question: Should a practitioner normally use performance data to compare themselves against other staff?

steps.body: Treat the metric definitions here as the supplied Splose descriptions, not Opal’s final word: exact calculation logic in Opal’s configuration, which metrics practitioners can see under current permissions, how managers will use targets, and how Splose revenue relates to the Opal Portal’s finance dashboards are all still to be confirmed.
steps.title: Still being finalised at Opal

steps.body:
You can find your report, do the utilisation sum, and read every metric for what it measures — with incomplete notes treated as the clinical to-do list it really is.

One module left: the whole workflow, end to end.
steps.title: Numbers in perspective

title: Set Up Your Splose Account
description: Your practitioner profile, the locations and services attached to it, and why a missing service is never solved by picking a different one.

steps.body:
Your practitioner profile controls three things: **where** you work, **which services** appear when a booking is made with you, and **when** you are available.

If any of those are wrong, bookings go wrong quietly — a service missing from a list, an appointment in the wrong location.

By the end of this lesson you can open My Account, check your locations and services, understand availability, and know exactly what to do when a service you need is not there.
steps.title: Why your profile matters

steps.body:
Click your **profile icon**, then open **My Account** and review your practitioner profile.

Two lists do the heavy lifting:

**Locations you work at** — the clinics and sites you can be booked into.

**Services provided by you** — the services that appear when someone books an appointment with you. A service only shows during booking when it is enabled for **both** you and the selected location.

The screenshot is from a Splose demo workspace — your real account shows Opal’s locations and service names.

image.alt: Splose practitioner settings showing a Locations you work at checklist and a Services provided by you checklist with a search box; several services are ticked and others left unticked. The organisatio

steps.title: Locations and services

steps.body:
Availability is when you are ordinarily open for work and bookings — it is **not** an appointment.

Splose availability can support recurring weekly patterns, fortnightly patterns, one-off days and custom hours. Review yours and set it according to your **Opal-approved work pattern**, then save and check the configuration.
steps.title: Availability

steps.body:
Do not tick every service just because the settings screen offers it — only use services appropriate to your profession, role and authorised configuration.

And if the service you need is **missing when you book**, never select a similar-looking service to make the booking work. A near-match creates wrong clinical and billing records.

Instead: check the selected **location**, check the service is assigned to **you**, and if it is still missing, contact **Opal administration**.
steps.title: Missing service? Never substitute

quiz.explain: Service visibility depends on the service + practitioner + location relationship. Check those first; if the right service still is not there, Opal administration fixes the assignment — a substitute service is never the answer.
options: Pick the closest similar service so the booking goes through
Check the selected location and your practitioner service assignment, then escalate to admin if it is still missing
Create the appointment as busy time and fix it later
quiz.question: You are booking a session and cannot find Telehealth OT in the service list. What do you do first?

quiz.explain: False — a wrong service means wrong records. Check the assignment, then escalate.
options: True
False
quiz.question: True or false: when the correct service is missing, selecting another similar service is acceptable.

quiz.explain: Availability is your ordinary working pattern — the frame bookings go into, not the bookings themselves.
options: The appointments already booked with you
When you are ordinarily available for work and bookings
Your leave calendar
quiz.question: What does your practitioner availability represent?

steps.body:
Before you move on, you should be able to tick every line:

✓ Splose login works
✓ Profile details reviewed
✓ Correct work locations visible
✓ Correct services for your role visible
✓ Availability reviewed against your approved pattern

Anything you cannot tick — raise it with Opal administration now, not on the morning of your first booking.

title: Your Splose Workflow at Opal
description: The capstone: a full day across Splose, Outlook and the Opal Portal, the decision drill, and the first-day checklist.

steps.body:
You have covered setup, booking, appointment changes, documentation, the Microsoft connection and your report. This capstone folds it into a single habit: for any task, you know **which system to open** without thinking.

Work through the day, drill the decisions, and finish with the first-day checklist.
steps.title: One mental model

steps.body:
**8:00** — Review Outlook for organisational meetings, with the subscribed Splose calendar alongside. Open Splose to confirm the authoritative participant appointments.

**9:00** — Home OT visit, booked in Splose. Attend, then complete the progress note in Splose; the Opal Portal handles the travel and invoice workflow.

**11:00** — Telehealth session booked in Splose; the Teams link was created through Splose. Deliver, then note in Splose.

**1:00** — Internal team meeting: Outlook/Teams.

**2:30** — A participant emails to move tomorrow’s session: reply in Outlook, reschedule in Splose, and the Outlook view catches up.

**End of day** — Check attendance statuses and incomplete notes in Splose; deal with travel and invoice tasks in the Opal Portal.

steps.body:
1. **Splose** is the clinical participant workflow and the source of truth for participant appointments.
2. **Outlook/Teams** is communication and meeting infrastructure.
3. **The Opal Portal** is the operational layer: travel, invoicing, resources, learning.
4. Never manage the same appointment in two systems.
5. When a workflow is unclear, do **not** invent a workaround that changes billing or clinical records — escalate to Opal administration or management.
steps.title: The five capstone rules

steps.body:
Before your first full week, every line should be true:

**Splose** — workspace invite accepted · login works · profile reviewed · correct locations visible · correct services visible · availability reviewed.

**Microsoft** — Opal Microsoft account working · Outlook working · Teams working.

**Splose + Microsoft** — Teams integration connected · calendar feed enabled if Opal requires it · Splose calendar subscribed in Outlook · and you understand the one-way sync.

**Opal Portal** — login works · Learning opens · travel, invoice and resource access as appropriate to your role.

If Opal has assigned you the Splose induction in Assigned Learning, its final knowledge check and checklist acknowledgement make this completion formal.
steps.title: The first-day checklist

steps.body:
That is the whole Splose induction: the right system for every task, appointments honest at their source of truth, documentation you stand behind, and a connected Microsoft setup that never confuses a view with the record.

Everything here stays available for review — and when a real case does not fit a rule you learned, that is a question for Opal administration, not a workaround.
